metadata.title: Situational Awareness, Hyperscaler Earnings and Warsh: A Bottom for AI Stocks?
metadata.speaker: Jordi Visser (solo weekly market update)

executive_takeaway: (1) A ~$45B AI-focused hedge fund, Situational Awareness (founded by Leopold Aschenbrenner), was forced to sell its entire public-equities book (~$16-20B) to Citadel (with Millennium also bidding) after running roughly 4x leverage into a July AI-stock rout that wiped out the equity behind its borrowed money — margin calls came from Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Bank of America. (2) Visser treats this forced unwind as a probable 'cleansing event' rather than the start of a bigger crisis, drawing on his own experience inside LTCM's 1998 closeout and the 2007 quant unwind — the key difference this time being that the two buyers (Citadel, Millennium) are themselves up big for the year and are considered strong risk managers, making a broader credit event less likely in his base case. (3) The damage was historic by several measures: the Goldman Sachs hedge-fund VIP basket had its worst month relative to the S&P since the index began in 2001 (worse than the Lehman month), tech momentum factors fell as much as 40% year-to-date at the Thursday low (worse than the dot-com bust), and momentum-factor realized volatility hit its highest level in the 45 years Visser has data for outside a recession. (4) Despite the carnage, Visser's own framework says the correction is largely over in price and time: 74-84% of his AI/thematic basket names remain above their 200-day moving averages, the 63-day rate of change round-tripped from +50% to -1.7%, and the S&P/Nasdaq have already staged textbook 'follow-through day' bounces off the panic low. (5) Q2 hyperscaler earnings (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta) all reinforced the 'compute demand is insatiable' thesis Visser has repeated weekly: combined backlog across Amazon/Google/Microsoft hit roughly $1.7T, and every hyperscaler CEO said demand still exceeds available capacity — directly contradicting the bearish narrative that this quarter would bring capex cuts. (6) Newly appointed Fed Chair Kevin Warsh held rates steady (3.50-3.75%) as expected, but market-structure volatility (not the Fed decision itself) was the real story of the week — Visser argues AI is 'compressing economic time,' making backward-looking risk models and terminal-value assumptions structurally unreliable, which is itself widening equity volatility versus index volatility. (7) On the All-In Podcast, David Sacks reportedly said Anthropic's annualized revenue reached roughly $74B through mid-2026 (implying ~10x growth this year) and OpenAI is pacing toward roughly $75B — a combined ~$175B in revenue from two companies that had none two years ago, which Visser uses to argue compute-demand skepticism is 'misleading.' (8) Visser flags the CCC/high-yield credit spread as the one indicator that could change his mind, name-checking unrelated private-credit stress (the Dodgers/Guggenheim/Mark Walter situation) as a reason to stay alert to contagion risk even while remaining structurally bullish on the AI trade.

conviction_map.topic: AI trade / hyperscaler capex & compute demand
conviction_map.action_status: HOLDING — reduced but not exited Micron, Marvell and other AI-basket names; added a little back this week
conviction_map.core_thesis: "Compute demand is insatiable" — repeated weekly since before the sell-off. Every hyperscaler (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta) said on Q2 earnings that demand exceeds available capacity; combined Amazon/Google/Microsoft backlog is ~$1.7T. Visser argues this directly refutes the bearish 'overbuilding, no revenue' narrative.
conviction_map.risks: He explicitly lost money this month and cut positions; own admission the correction may not be fully over — "not convinced yet that we've made the absolute low"

conviction_map.action_status: WATCHING — confirmed event, outcome (cleansing vs. beginning of bigger unwind) not yet resolved
conviction_map.core_thesis: Draws a direct historical parallel to LTCM (1998) and the 2007 quant unwind: once a distressed book gets 'marketed' to the street (shown to Citadel/Millennium), that itself completes the flush. Because the buyers are large, well-hedged, and up big for the year, he thinks this decompresses rather than cascades — his stated base case is no major credit event, just multiple compression and continued deleveraging.

conviction_map.topic: Structurally higher market volatility (post-AI regime change)
conviction_map.stance: POSITIVE VIEW (as a persistent regime, not a trade)
conviction_map.core_thesis: Tech-momentum and factor-neutral realized volatility have broken to structurally higher ranges (roughly 15-30 vs. 5-15 from 2000-2020) since ChatGPT-era AI began compressing 'terminal value' visibility for public companies; equity-level volatility has decoupled from and now sits meaningfully above index-level (VIX) volatility.
conviction_map.risks: This is Visser's own regime read from proprietary factor charts, not a market consensus view; he concedes he doesn't have comparable data going back further than 45 years

conviction_map.core_thesis: Fed held rates as expected; Visser frames Warsh as pushing to abandon backward-looking, frequently-revised economic data in favor of more forward-looking measures given how fast AI is moving — but treats the Fed decision itself as secondary to the market-structure story of the week.
conviction_map.risks: Speculative framing of Warsh's philosophy based on public remarks, not a specific tradeable call

technology_ai_views.theme: AI is compressing 'economic time' and destroying terminal-value visibility
technology_ai_views.view: Visser's central macro-structural argument (echoing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's comments on the All-In Pod): innovation cycles that used to take a decade now take about a year, so backward-looking valuation/risk models are structurally too slow, causing violent multiple compression even when earnings are fine.
technology_ai_views.companies: Adobe, Salesforce (named as terminal-value-uncertain examples); broadly all software/AI-exposed names
technology_ai_views.why: Explains why stocks can fall 40% with no change in earnings, and why hedge-fund risk models built on historical correlations are now unreliable.

technology_ai_views.theme: Token efficiency, not raw token output, is becoming the moat
technology_ai_views.view: Compute scarcity means the labs with the most efficient models per compute dollar can charge a premium and undercut competitors on delivered cost (his 'expensive gas → fuel-efficient car' analogy) — cites Anthropic's potential to let a company make a $5B-cost movie for a fraction of that via token efficiency.
technology_ai_views.companies: Anthropic, OpenAI, Moonshot AI (Kimi K3) as the cheap-but-less-efficient contrast case
technology_ai_views.why: Reframes the compute-scarcity bear case into a moat/pricing-power bull case for whoever already owns compute.

technology_ai_views.theme: Structurally higher, regime-shifted market volatility since AI-era compute build-out began
technology_ai_views.view: Factor-neutral and tech-momentum realized volatility has broken out of its 2000-2020 range (roughly 5-15) into a new 15-30+ range since around the ChatGPT era, and equity-level volatility has decoupled upward from index-level (VIX) volatility.
technology_ai_views.companies: Broad market / factor baskets, not single names
technology_ai_views.why: Argues prime brokers won't re-extend leverage back to pre-selloff levels even after this event resolves, keeping realized volatility structurally elevated.

technology_ai_views.theme: Hyperscaler compute demand still outstrips supply despite the sell-off narrative
technology_ai_views.view: Backlog across Amazon ($496B), Google (~$500-514B) and Microsoft (~$678-700B) totals roughly $1.7T; every hyperscaler CEO said on the Q2 2026 call that available capacity is the constraint, not demand.
technology_ai_views.why: Directly rebuts the 'AI overbuilding, capex cuts coming' bear case that Visser says drove much of the July sell-off.

ai_workflows.name: 'Combing through the rubble' — technical + fundamental re-entry screen
ai_workflows.goal: Systematically find AI-basket names that have been beaten down in price but remain structurally intact, to identify better risk/reward re-entry points after a sell-off.
ai_workflows.tools: Proprietary weekly technical sheet (uploaded to Visser's subscriber site); standard price/moving-average data
ai_workflows.approach: Screen for (1) price still above its 200-day moving average and (2) the 200-day moving average itself still sloping upward, then rank by how far the name has fallen on 30/60/90-day rate-of-change versus those two structural conditions; cross-check against reported fundamentals/earnings commentary before adding.
ai_workflows.why: Two structural conditions filter out names that are merely 'cheap' from names that are cheap *and* still in a structurally healthy uptrend — his stated favorite technical signal, also taught directly to RIAs.

ai_workflows.name: Rate-of-change (ROC) based position sizing for reducing/adding risk
ai_workflows.goal: Decide when to trim or add to a concentrated thematic position using price momentum extremes rather than trying to call exact tops/bottoms.
ai_workflows.tools: 63-day (≈3-month) and 30-day rate-of-change charts on a thematic portfolio/basket
ai_workflows.approach: Reduce risk when the trailing 63-day ROC reaches historic extremes (e.g., +50%); treat a full round-trip back toward flat/negative ROC, combined with elapsed time, as confirmation that 'price and time' consolidation requirements have been met before re-adding.
ai_workflows.why: Visser states markets move on a rate-of-change basis more than absolute price, and this method let him reduce Micron/Marvell exposure from mid-May onward ahead of the July drawdown, then re-enter smaller size afterward.

predictions.prediction: The Situational Awareness/Citadel-Millennium unwind marks a 'cleansing event' rather than the start of a broader hedge-fund/credit crisis
predictions.horizon: Next 6-7 trading days for initial confirmation; multi-week for full resolution
predictions.reasoning: Based on Visser's direct experience trading through LTCM (1998) and the 2007 quant unwind: once a large distressed book is shown to and absorbed by the largest, best-capitalized players (here, Citadel and Millennium, both up big for the year), that flush itself tends to mark the bottom rather than the start of contagion.
predictions.invalidated_by: A break below the panic-low support level; signs that additional highly-levered funds are being forced to unwind in the same window; credit spreads (especially CCC/junk) continuing to widen rather than stabilizing
predictions.assets: Broad AI/tech momentum basket, SMH, NDX

predictions.prediction: Markets will not fully re-lever or re-risk back to pre-selloff volatility levels even if the current scare passes
predictions.reasoning: Factor and tech-momentum realized volatility has broken into a structurally higher regime; prime brokers are unlikely to re-extend leverage to prior levels while this elevated volatility persists, and Visser doesn't expect volatility to compress quickly.
predictions.invalidated_by: A sustained return of factor-neutral realized volatility back to pre-2023 (roughly 5-15) ranges
predictions.assets: Tech momentum factor, factor-neutral long/short baskets, VIX vs. equity-vol spread

predictions.prediction: Micron re-rates back toward $1,500-1,600 over the next year
predictions.reasoning: DRAM prices have risen nearly every week since his 2016 baseline data began and continue rising; Visser sees a better risk/reward at current levels (~$850-900) versus where he trimmed in May, given the 200-day moving average (~$500) is well below spot.
predictions.invalidated_by: A sustained reversal in DRAM/memory pricing trends; Micron closing below its rising 200-day moving average

predictions.prediction: CCC/high-yield credit spreads are the indicator most likely to signal the next real risk event, ahead of equities
predictions.horizon: Unspecified — an ongoing watch-item, not a dated call
predictions.reasoning: Historically, credit stress starts in the weakest tier (CCC/junk) and 'drags everything in' afterward; Visser flags a 'bad-looking roll' in this spread alongside the private-credit/Dodgers-Guggenheim situation as early, unconfirmed signals worth monitoring.
predictions.invalidated_by: CCC/junk spreads stabilizing or tightening from current levels over the following weeks

notable_quotes.quote: Compute demand is insatiable. There is no way for the supply side to keep up with the demand of compute currently, and there are no indications that that's the case.
notable_quotes.speaker: Jordi Visser
notable_quotes.context: Opening thesis, repeated weekly across his videos, reasserted directly against this month's AI sell-off narrative.

notable_quotes.quote: I've lost money this month in a big way and my positions are reduced... but that's the market and that's what goes on.
notable_quotes.speaker: Jordi Visser
notable_quotes.context: Disclosing his own drawdown before laying out why he still thinks the broader AI thesis holds.

notable_quotes.quote: Once the marketing of the portfolio begins and they start looking for buyers, basically you're showing people other people's poker hands.
notable_quotes.speaker: Jordi Visser
notable_quotes.context: Explaining, from his own LTCM experience, why a distressed hedge-fund book being shopped to the street tends to complete rather than start a market flush.

notable_quotes.quote: Ubiquitous AI risk tools create a false sense of confidence. This is like watching people drive down the street with all-wheel drive when it's icy and snowy out, thinking that they're protected.
notable_quotes.speaker: Jordi Visser
notable_quotes.context: Warning that AI-driven portfolio-optimization tools are built on historical correlations that no longer hold in the current regime.

notable_quotes.quote: If gas is a dollar a gallon, nobody cares about the fuel efficiency. When it's $10, everyone pays a premium for the car with the best mileage.
notable_quotes.speaker: Jordi Visser
notable_quotes.context: Analogy for why token efficiency (not raw model capability) becomes the moat once compute is scarce and expensive.

notable_quotes.quote: Terminal value is gone forever... you're seeing things like companies that are private, like Anthropic, grow so fast, the fastest in the history of companies, but also seeing companies go out of business faster than they've ever.
notable_quotes.speaker: Jordi Visser
notable_quotes.context: Core structural argument for why traditional valuation models are breaking down across the market, not just in AI names.

notable_quotes.quote: How can you be arguing about ROIC when these guys are printing money at that side and the cloud revenue guys are printing $2 trillion during the exact same period?
notable_quotes.speaker: Jordi Visser
notable_quotes.context: Pushing back on bearish commentary questioning AI capex return-on-investment, citing combined lab + hyperscaler revenue growth.

risks: The claim that Anthropic's annualized revenue reached ~$74B through mid-2026 is attributed secondhand to David Sacks on the All-In Podcast and is notably higher than the ~$47B run-rate reported by independent outlets as of May 2026 — treat the exact figure as unverified/likely optimistic.

Visser explicitly discloses he lost money this month and reduced his own AI-basket positions — his bullish framing should be weighed against his own admitted drawdown and reduced conviction sizing (e.g., Micron position now ~1/5th its May size).

His base case that this is a 'cleansing event' rather than a broader unwind is explicitly a probability judgment, not a certainty — he states directly there could be another ~100 hedge funds in a similar leveraged position and that the unwind 'is definitely not over from people that need to get out.'

The video is a personal/subscriber market-commentary format; specific figures (e.g., Situational Awareness's exact leverage ratio, the precise size of the Citadel deal) are relayed from FT/WSJ-style reporting he read rather than primary-sourced by him directly — cross-check exact figures against original reporting before citing precisely.

Transcript is auto-generated from a ~62-minute solo monologue with fast, chart-heavy delivery; ticker/figure misattributions are possible (e.g., company names, percentage figures) — verify precise numbers before citing.

No explicit sponsorship disclosure appears in this transcript, but Visser repeatedly promotes his own subscriber-only 'thematic portfolio,' technical sheet, and RIA advisory conversations — his enthusiasm for the AI trade should be read alongside that commercial interest.

actionable_takeaways.item: Track whether more highly-levered AI-focused hedge funds face forced unwinds in the coming weeks — Visser's own base case (no broader credit event) depends on this NOT happening at scale.

Watch CCC/high-yield credit spreads, not just hyperscaler CDS — Visser flags this as the one indicator that could change his otherwise bullish read, and it's is easy to track via public credit-spread data.

When evaluating hyperscaler AI capex bear cases, check the actual backlog/RPO figures from the earnings call transcripts directly rather than secondhand commentary — Visser's cited numbers ($496B Amazon, ~$500-514B Google, ~$678-700B Microsoft) match independently reported Q2 2026 results.
Before repeating the '$74B Anthropic revenue' figure, verify against a primary source — it runs well ahead of the ~$47B run-rate reported elsewhere as of May 2026.

His 'combing through the rubble' screen (price above rising 200-day moving average, ranked by drawdown severity) is a reusable, mechanical way to find re-entry candidates after a sector-wide sell-off — applicable well beyond the AI trade.

glossary.definition: AI-focused hedge fund founded by Leopold Aschenbrenner that grew to ~$45B in assets and posted a 439% gain by June 2026 before being forced to sell its ~$16-20B public-equities book to Citadel after ~4x leverage was wiped out in July's AI-stock rout.

Goldman Sachs index tracking the most crowded/most-owned positions across the hedge-fund industry; used by Visser to show the worst relative monthly performance versus the S&P 500 since the index began in 2001.
A momentum indicator measuring the percentage price change over a fixed trailing window (Visser uses 30-day and 63-day); used here to time reductions/additions to concentrated thematic positions.

A technical-analysis signal (popularized by William O'Neil/IBD) confirming that an oversold bounce may be turning into a genuine rally rather than a short-covering pop, typically looked for 4-10 days after a low on rising volume.

A long/short basket constructed to strip out broad factor or sector exposure, isolating pure momentum performance; used by Visser to show the scale of the July momentum unwind independent of sector effects.
Contracted future revenue not yet recognized; cited for Amazon ($496B), Google (~$500-514B) and Microsoft (~$678-700B) as evidence hyperscaler demand still exceeds current capacity.
How much useful output/intelligence a model produces per unit of compute; Visser argues this — not raw model size — becomes the key competitive moat once compute is scarce and expensive.

The long-run valuation assumption for a company's cash flows beyond the explicit forecast period; Visser argues AI's pace of change makes terminal value far harder to estimate, driving multiple compression across software/tech.
